## What actually changed

Of 380 commits: 153 chore, 73 refactor, 64 test, 33 ci, 20 docs — that's 88% with zero user-visible surface. The real content is **1 feature, 11 distinct fixes, and 3 things you'll want to call breaking.**

The fix and refactor subjects repeat across scopes (e.g. "guard the null cursor in the paginator" lands 4 times in queue, api, webhooks, db). I collapsed those into one line each — a user experiences one behavior change, not four.

## Three judgment calls I made

**1. I promoted three items to Breaking that aren't marked breaking.** No commit carries a `!` or `BREAKING CHANGE` footer, so a marker-based read of this log yields an empty Breaking section. But:

- `fix(auth): return 401 for an expired token instead of 403` is filed as a fix and is one, but it changes a status code on a public endpoint. Anyone with error handling keyed to 403 breaks silently.
- `refactor(*): stop re-exporting the internal error types` — 8 commits across core, db, auth, jobs, billing. "Internal" is the maintainers' view; if those symbols were reachable from a package entry point, removing them breaks imports. **This is the one I'd most want you to verify** — check whether the removed exports were in the published surface. If they only ever moved between `src/` files, delete that bullet.
- `refactor(api): drop the unused v1 export route` (#4152 / 56dc828) touched `router.js`, `handlers.js`, and `test/api.test.js`. "Unused" per the author, but you can't observe a caller's usage from inside the repo. If you have route telemetry, confirm before shipping this as a silent removal.

**2. I dropped all 10 perf commits.** Your template is fixed at three headings, and the perf work is generic micro-optimization (skip a JSON round-trip, avoid a clone, batch metric writes) with no measured numbers attached. Nothing an installer would notice. If you have benchmark figures, say the word and I'll add a heading.

**3. I called out the histogram fix as a data discontinuity.** `use the right units in the latency histogram` means previously recorded values were wrong. Anyone with dashboards or alert thresholds on that metric sees a step change on upgrade. That's worth more than a one-liner if you have users alerting on it.

Also worth knowing: `fix(db): stop logging the whole request body` is a privacy fix — request bodies were going to logs. If those logs went anywhere retained or shared, that may need handling beyond a changelog line.

## Two things to check before you publish

**The history stops on 2026-06-17.** Both files end there — that's about ten weeks before tomorrow's cut. Either the branch genuinely froze in June, or the export was taken then and there's unseen work. If commits landed after 6/17, this digest is incomplete and I can redo it against a fresh log.

**Minimum Node version may have moved.** Five `docs: note the minimum node version` commits, three `.nvmrc` pins, and a `ci: run the suite on node 22` all point at a bump — but every one touches docs or CI, never a `package.json` engines field. I didn't add it, because asserting a version I can't see would be a bad install-time surprise. Check `engines`; if it changed, that's a fourth Breaking bullet.

Dependency bumps are all patch/minor (pino, zod, fastify, pg, knex, dotenv, ioredis, nanoid, undici at runtime; the rest dev-only). Nothing there reaches a user, so nothing is listed.
